fields.title: Retention: users return for value, not reminders
fields.keyTakeaway: Re-engagement mechanics amplify value that already exists; they don't create it out of nowhere. First find the natural frequency of the task, then build a reason to return at that exact moment.
fields.checkQuestion: A product is needed once a quarter. What will a daily notification achieve?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how to retain users until payback?**
fields.blocks/1/text: The key phrase here is "until payback". Retention isn't needed for its own sake: a customer must stay long enough to recover their acquisition cost. This links this node to CAC and LTV calculations.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Four steps of a single retention loop
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Trigger** — external (notification, email) or internal (a situation where the user naturally remembers the product). The goal is converting external into internal.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Action** — the simplest valuable action. The higher the effort required, the less frequently the loop completes.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Variable reward** — an outcome that isn't identical every time: a new response, a updated number, a change in state.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Investment** — users leave something of their own in the product: data, settings, history. Every subsequent visit becomes more valuable and switching away becomes harder.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Natural frequency: issuing invoices 2–4 times a month, certificates at month-end, reporting once a quarter.

What failed: daily "what's new" summary. 4% open rate, 12% unsubscribed.

What worked: email on the 25th "time to close the month" with a list of unsigned certificates. 47% open rate, 31% return to the product.

The difference is that the second aligns with the moment when the need naturally arises — rather than trying to create it artificially.
fields.blocks/4/text: **Investment is the most underrated part.** Saved counterparty details, templates, and signature history make the product their own. That's why data import during onboarding is often more important than any retention mechanic.
fields.blocks/5/text: A notification that doesn't align with a task costs more than it seems: it isn't just ignored, it trains users to ignore all future ones.
fields.blocks/5/title: Retention mechanics easily turn into annoyance
fields.blocks/6/text: The Hook Model describes products with a high-frequency cycle. For infrequent tasks, it's more honest to build a reliable presence at the right moment rather than a habit — and measure retention by quarters, not days.
